item.title: A Closer Examination of SCP-173: Re: A Closer Examination of SCP-173
item.content:encoded:
[+] Overall
[-] Overall

I actually kinda like this. There's some tonal issues that I've talked about in more depth but it actually like…provides an interesting take on 173 that feels supported by the evidence of the files and like makes logical sense.

My one thought is it feels like this should produce testable hypothesis so that it can be proven/disproven; but I don't necessarily think the absence is a huge issue.

I'm a little unsure whether the framing device works here; the framing is nice but it feels inconsequential and idk, I'm not necessarily sure if it'd work just as well without it? Or alternatively, whether it'd work better if it came up more and broke up the relatively long technical section more?

Either way, I would strongly recommend getting a bunch of opinions on this: this feels very much like the kind of work that might be very hit or miss and moving this as much as possible towards hit would be a good idea.

[-] Overall
[+] Line By Line
[-] Line By Line

Gonna note that I can miss stuff; flag things which are right as being wrong and indeed flag things which are deliberately wrong.
I'll likely use strikethrough to indicate stuff to remove and green text to indicate stuff to add.

So it's only the best-known skip we have. Even the D-Class know its file from memory.

This feels like an odd line; like…out of universe, the assessment that 173 is the best known SCP is accurate but in-universe, it feels weird that there'd even be a best known SCP because of Foundation infosec restricting stuff as much as possible?

The Moose won't even read another Peanut paper.

I feel like this should be like 'Director Moose'; and I'm not necessarily sure that in-universe, people would refer to 173 as 'peanut'

"We've come a long way since 1993."

this kinda feels a little iffy solely because we don't actually have a framing for when this is: it could be 1994 or it could be 30004, y'know?

"SCP-173 is animate and extremely hostile. The object cannot move while within a direct line of sight."

I'd probably nest this in a quote block inside the quote block e.g.:

SCP-173 is animate and extremely hostile. The object cannot move while within a direct line of sight.

These two sentences are the most important pieces of information in SCP-173's file.

The same goes whenever you quote from the 173 file in general here

But we still take it for granted.

This is a scientific report; generally you're aiming for passive voice a lot and like…statements of fact, rather than opinion? This phrasing makes it feel more like an op-ed in a newspaper than a scientific journal paper; and it feels inappropriate to me but I'm not exactly sure what the purpose of this report is so?

under observation. the issue with this

missing capital

it is SCP-187's response to the object. A moving statue is not something that sends anyone into a two-day coma.

I feel like this is a little…awkwardly phrased? It doesn't quite cover the flow of information in a way that inherently makes sense, particularly if you aren't familiar with 187

During the containment breach on ██/██/████, D-████ was able to evade SCP-173

The framing implies this report is being written as we are reading it; which in turn implies the author of the report inserted these as black boxes instead of like…writing in a date and a d-class number.

My inclination even without the framing would be to show this data and just pick stuff; no-one will call you out for writing about a containment breach on a certain date

It is possible to catch brief glimpses of SCP-372, but (as I said earlier) this is not the case with 173

I don't think the '(as I said earlier)' is necessary here since you just said it; like if this had been covered a few paragraphs ago, sure but it's like, three lines ago.

So at the start you say:

SCP-173's composition and form change when it is unobserved, SCP-173 does not "move" in the typical sense of the word, and SCP-173 possesses limited precognitive abilities.

and yet here you say:

However, I do not believe that SCP-173 is a shapeshifting, teleporting, precognitive entity.

These two positions are opposites and you really gotta clear up which one it is.

[-] Line By Line

item.title: Life Is But A Dream: Re: Life Is But A Dream
item.content:encoded:
[+] Overall
[-] Overall

There's a delightful kinda fridge logic to the realisation that the world of SCP is a dream likely being had by Isabelle Wondertainment; but it feels…like this obfuscates it too much for the realisation to feel like a shock; and it also feels like even if it didn't, it'd feel like this was missing something?

I believe the implication here is also that Isabelle created the Foundation? Or is it just that she dreamed about the Foundation and then decided to make a play set from this? I feel like if it's the second, this is just…really missing something and idk what; maybe just the purple section needs to really characterise her more than it does currently?

It's possible that what this needs is a test or two which shows what this does before the test that shows Isabelle doing stuff; like, really establish an expectation for what this does before breaking the expectation with the purple note at the end?

[-] Overall
[+] Line By Line
[-] Line By Line

Gonna note that I can miss stuff; flag things which are right as being wrong and indeed flag things which are deliberately wrong.
I'll likely use strikethrough to indicate stuff to remove and green text to indicate stuff to add.

is contained within a secure pharmaceutical locker 2A at Site-██.

Why is the Site redacted? Like who has clearance to look at this file and know exactly what it is but not where it is?

SCP-XXXX is a number of gummy candies, stored inside a plastic pill jar.

How many gummy candies? Or rather, this really feels like it needs an indication of whether this is like…a handful of candies or like, 3 candies, or like, 3000, y'know? You could specify via mass instead of exact count but *shrugs*.

Instances (SCP-XXXX-1) are coloured purple and each engraved with the digits “001” on one side, and a capitalised “W” on the other.

I'm looking at this work as a whole and seeing you use -1 a lot, and the base anomaly not much and it feels like perhaps the designations need reworking: ideally I'd suggest not using a designation for both the collective and the individual, perhaps in the style of e.g. SCP-500

including permanent loss of brain functionality or splintering of the neural consciousness.

this feels…weird. Idk, on the one hand, Wondertainment feels like they'd avoid releasing pills that do this; and on the other, it feels somewhat like an unclinical way to phrase it, particularly the 'splintering of the neural consciousness' line.

On the bottom of the jar is written “IHAPW” is written in blue marker.

I'm not exactly clear on the significance of these letters: it seems like it's a reference to Isabelle Wondertainments name? Perhaps it'd be worth showing that here?

before experiencing SCP-XXXX-2.

You haven't explained what -2 is yet so this is meaningless; I'd either cut this bit and note at the start of the next paragraph that they experience -2 during this time or add a short explanation of what happens (e.g. "fall asleep shortly afterwards, before experiencing an 8 minute long lucid dream (designated SCP-XXXX-2)").

Limited testing has confirmed SCP-XXXX-2 to be apparently near-identical to the real world, including locations and living entities indistinguishable to their actual counterparts; full exploration of SCP-XXXX-2 has yet to be achieved. Subjects will appear as a different person other than themselves each time arriving in SCP-XXXX-2; within the present location of the person’s real-world counterpart.

Something about this phrasing feels…awkward? I can't put my finger on it but it feels like it's kinda…obfuscating the point a lot and making it needlessly complex.

the dream will always end with the subject consuming SCP-XXXX-1A.

SCP-XXXX-1A is the respected instances SCP-XXXX-1 located within SCP-XXXX-2.

This explanation is also very confusing, and the introduction of the designation before the meaning for the designation isn't ideal.

Addendum - Continued Testing Log:

Is this section finished? The way it cuts to like, the purple section at the end feels weird; like there's a whole bunch of the file that hasn't been written in between and yet, the purple section directly follows off it so??

[-] Line By Line

item.title: The Click: Re: The Click
item.content:encoded:
Wouldn't you agree that the majority of people who work for the Foundation fit this bill in some form or fashion?

Personally, no, I would definitely disagree with the statement. I would hope that the Foundation recruits in a manner that would result in the majority of their staff not having PTSD-triggering memories at all—counseling and therapy take up resources, and bring down employee morale overall. Granted, I've never been a fan of the grimdark approach to the Foundation, so if you want to write this for the portion of the audience that willingly believes that the majority of Foundation staff have dark pasts and traumatic memories, it's your prerogative.

+ show block
– hide block

The anomaly mind-melds the affected subjects into one mental being with two bodies, hence the final line. The resulting entity had all of the combined resentment of authority, trauma, and guilt from both individuals, and thus bided its time until it could dispatch Dr. Pollock effectively. Via the lip-reading section, this is implied to be retaliation for some unspeakable thing that occurred to SCP-XXXX-1B in the past.

For something like this, you'd probably be better off just putting it right in the description. An incident as significant as this in comparison with the conditions/states of the anomaly would be priority knowledge for anyone having to handle the anomaly. There's no point burying in a collapsed log with roundabout cryptic dialogue.

Although… as a reader, I'm still left with the "so what?" reaction. Why does the anomaly mind-meld people? How is the reader supposed to react to the kind of randomly added murder of Pollock, which seems kind of shoehorned in for shock value?

Isn't the fact that it can occur anywhere unpredictably enough to classify it as keter?

Does the Foundation have any confirmed evidence that the anomaly as observed in the Foundation staff occurs similarly elsewhere in the world? The way the article is set up, it seems solely focused on the one Foundation-based case, with no mention of the effects being noticed elsewhere. "It could spontaneously occur anywhere" and "there could be more of these things out there" aren't good enough to justify Keter designation if the in-universe Foundation is relying solely on extrapolation.

item.title: The Click: Re: The Click
item.content:encoded:
Mirroring Sun’s notes above, the dialogue is wooden and we never really get a handle on who these people are or why we should care that they’re affected in this way

Leading from that, this has a lack of real stakes. In all but one recorded instance the individuals eventually move on and don’t recall anything anomalous (so it’s not really even a threat to the Veil)… but why would the foundation expend time and effort in this detailed a report? More importantly, why would the reader stay engaged?

Without real stakes and characters, this feels very flat.

On a separate note: the crossing out and the black boxes really don’t make sense. As the meta means we’re (as readers) able to can access to the file so why would anything be redacted?

Ask yourself: “if the reader knew what was behind the black box, would it matter?” I think the answer is no, and so they shouldn’t be used. Certainly not the amount of which you have done so

The crossing out is another thing, this is a digital file, so crossing out makes no sense. You can communicate those changes: “it was originally thought that long term containment was impossible but given the events as laid out in ___, this is no longer the case.”
